name: Ottoman classical army: janissaries and timariot sipahis (1450-1683)

weightNotes.aggression: Sultan-led campaigns almost every year of the classical period: Constantinople 1453, Chaldiran 1514, Mohacs 1526, Vienna 1529 and 1683 (Agoston, Last Muslim Conquest; battle pages). The army usually forced the enemy to attack prepared positions, so tactically less aggressive than strategically.
weightNotes.maneuver: Armies of 60,000-100,000 with 300 guns (Mohacs page) moved slowly along prepared roads; manoeuvre was by akinci raiders and the cavalry wings, not the main body (Murphey, Ottoman Warfare). Middling-low.
weightNotes.flanking: Battle plans used the cavalry wings against the enemy flanks: Anatolian cavalry ambushed the crusader flank at Varna (1444); at Mohacs the Ottomans 'launched a counterattack with cavalry and light infantry from both wings' (Varna, Mohacs pages).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Campaign objectives were fortresses: Constantinople (1453), Rhodes (1522), Belgrade (1521), Szigetvar (1566), Vienna (1529, 1683). Heavy artillery and sapping were core skills (Agoston, Guns for the Sultan). High.
weightNotes.reserveUse: The sultan's household troops, janissaries and artillery, stood in the centre behind carts and ditches while provincial cavalry fought on the wings; the janissaries were the last-line reserve that stopped Wladyslaw's charge at Varna (Varna page). Moderate.
weightNotes.scouting: Akinci light horse screened and raided ahead, and pre-war intelligence was good; but at Vienna 1683 Kara Mustafa failed to prepare for the relief army and left the rear to the Crimean Tatars (Vienna page). Middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Share of the engaged force lost before it withdrew or broke. Vienna 1683: an Ottoman list records 48,544 casualties by 10 September out of an army Sakul estimates at about 120,000 (about 40%, siege attrition included) before the army broke under the relief army's charge on 12 September (Vienna page). The janissary centre was not broken in the victories at Varna 1444, Chaldiran 1514 and Mohacs 1526 (battle pages). Saint Gotthard 1664: losses fell 'mostly on the elite corps', no share given. The timariot cavalry broke contact earlier, with no figure. 0.3.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Artillery, musket-armed janissaries behind a cart barrier, sipahi lancer-archers on the wings and akinci raiders (Chaldiran: 'heavy artillery and thousands of Janissaries equipped with gunpowder weapons behind a barrier of carts'; Agoston). Among the most integrated armies of the 16th century.
weightNotes.initiative: Highly centralised under the sultan or grand vizier, with the Rumelian and Anatolian provincial contingents on the wings to a set plan (Varna page; Murphey). Little evidence of subordinate latitude.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Stockpiles and road stations prepared before each campaign (Vienna 1683: roads and bridges repaired and ammunition forwarded in advance, Vienna page); an army of 60,000 men and 40,000 horses needed half a million kg of food per day (Military of the Ottoman Empire page). Campaigns ended with the season (Murphey). High.

summary: A two-part army: the sultan's salaried household (janissary musketeers, artillery corps, household cavalry) and the far larger provincial cavalry of timariot sipahis, lancer-archers paid by land grants, plus akinci raiders and auxiliaries. In battle the janissaries and guns stood behind chained carts and ditches in the centre (the tabur), the provincial cavalry fought on the wings and drew the enemy onto the guns, and the household reserve finished the fight. Campaigns were prepared a year ahead with stockpiles and road stations and aimed at a key fortress, taken by artillery and mining.
whyItWorked: Scale, logistics and firepower: no European state could field 300 guns and a standing musket infantry in the 16th century (Mohacs page; Agoston). The tabur defence turned the enemy's attack into a killing ground (Chaldiran 1514 against Safavid cavalry without guns; Mohacs 1526, Hungarian lines collapsed within two hours). Siege artillery and engineers took Constantinople, Belgrade and Rhodes.
whereItFailed: Distance and season: Vienna in 1529 and 1683 lay at the end of the campaign radius; in 1683 a two-month siege left the army weak and demoralised and the relief army's cavalry routed it in under three hours. Western armies that held firm against the cavalry and out-fired the janissaries won (Saint Gotthard 1664 under Montecuccoli). By the 17th century timar cavalry was declining and the janissaries were politicised.
